title: From Writing Code to Designing Systems: How the Developer Role is Changing — Chris Noring, Microsoft
talk_summary: Chris Noring argues the developer's entry point is shifting from editor to CLI, with agents delegated to sandboxes that return draft PRs for human review. He frames scaling as requiring guardrails: AGENTS.md for repo intent, skills as constrained repeatable recipes, and custom agents as tool-limited orchestrators.

takeaways.what_they_do: Package repeatable multi-step procedures as a folder with a SKILL.md (front matter name/description + markdown instructions) so agents invoke a fixed recipe instead of improvising.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a skill is called by an agent, it has a strict contract, it's self-contained because it just lives in a folder

takeaways.what_they_do: A high-level repo file stating intent, architecture, constraints, and explicit don'ts (e.g., don't change architecture unprompted), present in every repo.
Define agents with a persona plus an explicit tool allowlist (e.g., a researcher that can read/search web but not edit files), constraining what each role can do.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Tools is an important concept, because that's able to constrain the agent what it can do or not

takeaways.what_they_do: Delegate a task to an agent running in an isolated sandbox that cannot escape but can open a draft PR, making the PR the human-in-the-loop approval gate.

takeaways.technique: Issue-assigned delegation to fill idle capacity
takeaways.what_they_do: Assign issues directly to agents from the tracker UI so a backlog of small issues can be dispatched in parallel while humans do other work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Each of these issues are a next feature or a bug fix... Delegate, delegate, delegate, and I go have a coffee

takeaways.technique: Human merge gate after agent draft PR
takeaways.what_they_do: Agents propose draft PRs; humans retain merge authority and can add approval gates, rather than letting agents merge autonomously.
